title: Designed to Be Seen
objective: Students will see toy design as a set of choices about who is shown. They will compare Francie, *“essentially a white doll design with darker skin,”* with the first Black Barbie, designed by Kitty Black Perkins with *“Afrocentric facial features, natural hairstyles, and a glamorous design that celebrated Black beauty.”* Then they will design a doll of their own and explain each choice.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Every toy, book and poster is designed by someone, and every choice decides who is shown. In 1980 a Black designer, Kitty Black Perkins, made different choices, and her doll inspired further diversification in the toy industry.

materials: *Who Do You See?*, *Design a doll* tab (online), projected
Colored pencils, with a range of skin tones
Page 3 of this plan; differentiated handouts
questions: What is the difference between recoloring a design and designing from the start?
Whose idea of beauty did the original Barbie carry? How do you know?
Which choice in the *Design a doll* tab surprised you? Who does it include?
Poster 1 puts a musician, a singer, a worker and a scientist in its ring. Who would you put in yours?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **Online,** the *Design a doll* tab lets students build a doll, name it, and save or print it. **In the exhibition,** compare the dolls in the display case: the Nigerian and Ghanaian boxed editions and the three Inspiring Women dolls.

steps.title: Seven ways to wear it
script: Show seven of the natural hairstyles from the *Design a doll* tab: Afro, Afro puffs, Bantu knots, box braids, cornrows, locs and twists. Ask: *“What do you notice? Why would a toy designer offer all of these?”* Draw out that every option is a decision someone made, and that a missing option is a decision too.

steps.purpose: Look before being told: a design choice decides who is shown.
students: Why would a toy designer offer all of these?

steps.title: Two designs
script: Read poster 2’s two sentences side by side (page 3). Francie was *“essentially a white doll design with darker skin.”* The first Black Barbie, designed by Kitty Black Perkins, *“a trailblazing Black fashion designer at Mattel,”* featured *“Afrocentric facial features, natural hairstyles, and a glamorous design that celebrated Black beauty.”* Ask: *what is the difference between changing one color and designing from the start?*

screen.text:
Francie, 1967:
“essentially a white doll design with darker skin”

The first Black Barbie, 1980:
“Afrocentric facial features, natural hairstyles, and a glamorous design that celebrated Black beauty”

steps.purpose: See the difference between changing one color and designing from the start.
students: What did Francie’s designers change? What did they keep?
What did Kitty Black Perkins design differently?

steps.title: The choices
script: Open the *Design a doll* tab and try a few choices together: skin tone, hair, head covering, extras such as glasses, a hearing aid or a prosthetic leg, a wheelchair, and clothes. Ask: *who does each choice include?*

screen.alt: The Who Do You See? room: a doll being designed on a pink card, with choices of hair, face and skin tone
screen.caption: *Who Do You See?* · Design a doll

steps.purpose: List the choices a designer can make, and who each one includes.
students: Name five choices a doll designer makes.

steps.title: Designed to be seen
script: Show poster 1. Its designer made choices too: a ring of circular vignettes of a musician, a singer, a worker and a scientist; an acid lime ground; heavy, wide capitals. Ask: *what do these choices say about who and what is celebrated?*

screen.alt: Poster 1, Black History Month, on an acid lime ground: a ring of circular illustrated vignettes — a musician, a singer at a microphone, a worker in a cap and a scientist at a microscope, music notes and an atom — around a black shape lettered Black History Month, above three paragraphs of text
screen.caption: Poster 1 · *Black History Month*

steps.purpose: Read a poster’s design choices the way we read a doll’s.
students: Who is in the ring of circles?
What do the colors and lettering say?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three design a doll and explain the choices.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Label the design choices on a drawn doll, then design one: a natural hairstyle, a skin tone from the swatches, clothes and one more choice; finish *I chose… because…*

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare Francie’s design with the first Black Barbie’s, plan a doll on a design sheet (skin tone, hair, clothes, one extra), draw it, and write a designer’s statement.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Explain what “conventional beauty standards” are and how a design can challenge them, design a doll and its box front in a poster’s style, and write an artist’s statement that cites the poster.

steps.purpose: Design with purpose, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three design a doll and explain the choices.

steps.title: Gallery walk
script: Lay the designs out. Students walk, look and leave one sticky note on a design naming a choice that widens who can see themselves. Ask two designers to read their statements.

screen.question: Which design choice in our gallery widens who can see themselves?

steps.purpose: See each other’s designs, and name the choices that matter.
students: Walk, look, and leave one note on a design.
Name a choice that widens who is shown.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Ask one student to answer each aloud; for the last, ask a Red Level reader.
